_comment: Curated public-site capture lane: stable, login-free, bot-tolerant sites with hand-authored hard tasks. Tasks must be NON-DESTRUCTIVE (browse/search/navigate/configure-view only — no account creation, no posting, no purchases). Phrase instructions as user intents robust to cosmetic UI changes; the verifier judges the final screenshot, so every task must end in a visually checkable state.

tasks.instruction: Find the Wikipedia article about the Voyager 1 spacecraft, then navigate from it to the article about the rocket that launched it, ending with that rocket's article on screen.
Look up the article 'List of countries by population' and sort or locate the table so that the country ranked 5th by population is visible on screen.
Search Wikipedia for 'Mercury', open the disambiguation page, and navigate to the article about the chemical element, ending on its physical properties section.
Open today's featured article from the Wikipedia main page, then view its edit history and end with the list of recent changes to it on screen.
Look up the article about the Eiffel Tower and switch it to the German edition, ending with the German article visible.
From Wikipedia's main page, pick an event from the 'On this day' section, open its article, and end on the references section.
Find the article about chess, open its categories at the bottom, and navigate into the 'Chess' category page, ending with its subcategories visible.
Search Open Library for books by Ursula K. Le Guin, filter the results to show only ebooks, and open the page for one of them.
Browse to the science fiction subject page and narrow what is shown to works from the 1960s, ending with the filtered list visible.
I want to see which has more works listed on Open Library: Isaac Asimov or Arthur C. Clarke — check both author pages and end on the one with more.
Find the trending books section on Open Library, open the most-trending title, and end on its ratings area.
Search for Lisbon, Portugal, then pan the map westward by dragging until the Atlantic coastline is centered, ending zoomed in enough to read street names near the waterfront.
Use the directions feature to get a route from 'Gare du Nord, Paris' to 'Gare de Lyon, Paris', ending with the route summary visible.
Find Tokyo on the map, then switch the base layer to the cycling map, ending with Tokyo shown in the new layer.
Find Iceland on the map and zoom in by dragging and scrolling until Reykjavik's street grid is readable, ending centered on the city.
Look at Venice, Italy on the map close enough to see its canals, then jump to Amsterdam and end at a comparable zoom over its canal ring.
Find books by Jules Verne available in French on Project Gutenberg, and open the book page for one of them, ending with its download options visible.
Show me what's popular: open Project Gutenberg's most-downloaded books list and open the page for whichever ranks first today.
Find Project Gutenberg's detective fiction bookshelf and open a book from it, ending with the book's reading options visible.
Search the Internet Archive for 'Apollo 11', filter the results to show only videos, sort them by date, and open one result, ending on its item page.
Browse to the MS-DOS games collection on the Internet Archive, sort by most viewed all time, and open the top result's page.
Use the Wayback Machine on archive.org to look up how nytimes.com looked, and open a snapshot from any year before 2010.
Find the MDN reference page for the CSS 'grid-template-areas' property and scroll to its interactive example, ending with the example visible.
flexbox guide — find MDN's main flexbox layout guide (not the property reference) and end at its section about wrapping.
I keep seeing 418 jokes — find MDN's page explaining HTTP status code 418 and end with its description on screen.
Look up the word 'serendipity' on Wiktionary, read its etymology, and follow the link to the word it derives from, ending on that entry.
Find the Wiktionary entry for 'butterfly' and expand its translations section so the Japanese translation is visible.
Look up 'orange' on Wiktionary and navigate to its rhymes page, ending with the rhymes list visible.
Search Open Food Facts for breakfast cereals and narrow the results to products with Nutri-Score A, ending with the filtered list on screen.
Look up Nutella on Open Food Facts and end on the section of its product page that lists additives.
Browse Open Food Facts' chocolate category, narrow it to products sold in Germany, and open the first product, ending on its Nutri-Score detail.
